title: The Green Revolution
hookLine: Punjab's farms fed India, at a cost to water and soil

cards: A sack of grain sits on a scale in a market yard, and a farmer in a turban watches the needle. Behind him, a tractor. Behind the tractor, a field of wheat so even it looks combed.
Under the field, a pipe going down into the ground, pulling up water. The seed, the machine, the pipe: each of them changed Punjab. The change got a big name, the Green Revolution.
Its harvest fed a country. Its bill is still being paid in water and in soil.

teach.b: First, the seeds. New kinds of wheat, and then rice, gave far bigger harvests, as long as they had plenty of water and fertilizer. Punjab had rivers, canals and farmers ready to try them.
Its grain went into the government's stores and out to the rest of India. Second, the farmer.

At Ang 595 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak borrows the farmer's year for the inner life: make the mind the plowman, good deeds the farming, effort the water and the body the field, and sow the Name as the seed.
Tradition says Guru Nanak himself worked the fields in his later years. A Punjab farmer's whole day is already inside that hymn. Third, the cost.
Rice is thirsty, and Punjab's own rains could not water it. Farmers sank tube wells deeper and deeper, and the water underground began to fall.

teach.h: THE WATER FALLS, THE SOIL TIRES.
teach.b: Fertilizer and pesticide built up in the soil and the water. Some families took on debt for machines and seed.
Farmers, scientists and Sikh groups have all raised the alarm, and not all of them agree on what should change. Fourth, the root.

teach.h: ANG 8: WATER THE FATHER, EARTH THE MOTHER.
teach.b: In the closing verse of Japji, at Ang 8, Guru Nanak calls air the guru, water the father, and the earth the great mother.
Spoken beside a well that has to be dug deeper every few seasons, that line reads less like poetry and more like plain description.
The Green Revolution is a story of a huge gift, and a question about how to thank the ones who gave it.

how: Sikh families across Punjab farm, and gurdwaras and Sikh groups have joined farmers and scientists in campaigns about falling groundwater and the health of Punjab's soil.

games.q: you farm in Punjab. the new rice pays well, but your well has to go deeper every few seasons. what do you do?
o: keep planting rice and dig deeper.
switch to crops that need less water.
there's no single answer: the choice is hard.
games.why: farmers face exactly this, and not everyone agrees on the answer. the harvest that fed a nation is tied to the water it drew.

practice: Put your feet flat on the floor, or a hand on a plant, or just picture a field.

Think of the last thing you ate and trace it back, the shop, the truck, the farmer, the field, the water under the field, naming one with each breath in and thanking it with each breath out, all the way down to the soil.
If you pray, let each thank-you be a Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Green Revolution. New seeds, water and machines that turned Punjab's fields into a granary for India, at a cost to its water and its soil. Today's word.
